citations.review_text: Cutscreen simulator. Leave the HQ (cutscreen) run to the UC offices to take the elevator down (cutscreen) you took the elevator down to get on a metro transit thingy (cutscreen) to get to the center part of town to run to your ship where via a (cutscreen) you get to space so you can via another cutscreen use your grav drive to get to another solar system where via ANOTHER cut screen you land on a planet where you walk through a door that gives you yet another cut screen. GIVE ME A BREAK MAN.

I enjoyed my time playing Starfield. I like the Bethesda style of being able to mess around in the world, joining factions and participating in world altering storylines

In Starfield, exploration is not as cohesive as in Elder Scrolls and Fallout it must be said. There may be 1000 odd planets but each planet does not have that much to explore and exploration can be more menu driven compared to Bethesda's other games where you could go travel the world in any direction you choose.

That aside, I enjoyed the various sidequests and faction plots, with Sysdef/Crimson Fleet being the standout faction-wise featuring double agency, piracy, potential treasure and a fun time. A lot of the sidequests feel interesting to play on a first-time playthrough; stuff like meeting a rogue AI, figuring out what to do with a bunch of early explorers out of earth, uncovering the mystery of a vigilante hero are some ones off the top of my head which I liked. I might make it sound cooler than these quests were in the game, but I felt there were different and interesting sub stories in the game.

The game also has mission board style quests where you have repeatable quests for bounty hunting, delivering goods and maybe for other jobs that I don't remember. They mostly play in the same standard way, but if you feel comfortable having that game loop where you can roleplay as a bounty hunter or a trader, you can do it to some extent.

I liked the main quest, I didn't really like the idea of the story being hunting artifacts at first, but as the story progressed to the Starborn and the stakes seemed to get more serious for Constellation, I warmed up to it. I liked Constellation, from the 4 companions to the homebodies, they were a cool main cast and I wish the game featured Matteo and Noel a bit more tbh. The story does get piled on usually and the Starborn temple puzzles could have been more interesting, but IMO its a nice enough storyline that does its job of feeling high-stakes and grandios…

citations.review_text: Completely unplayable. It stutters every few seconds and just crashes on occasion. I got this game about 2 years ago and I could play it fine then; but not now. I have no clue how Bethesda could have ruined this game, when it ran fine when I played it at first. I came back to it hoping to actually beat it since I became focused on other games then. I really hope they somehow fix this buggy mess.

Disclaimer: standard Bethesda bugginess applies.  Starfield may crash a lot on some systems especially as one plays over longer stretches of time.  This is my second copy of the game, the other being on console.

I do recommend this game, but not as originally released.  Starfield has a lot of emptiness to it and I don't mean just in outer space.  Bethesda seemingly designed Starfield with the idea of harnessing a paid mod marketplace and so left room for enterprising mod authors to add their own content and tweaks.  However, once you add Bethesda's Shattered Space, Terran Armada, and Trackers Alliance expansions the game does fill out enough to justify purchasing and playing (grab it all during a sale).  

Once you have played through Bethesda's content I recommend giving serious consideration to mods (both free and paid) that have been thoroughly reviewed on Youtube.  For example: Watchtower retails for about $10 and expands the game with fleet command, orbital strikes, and giant mech enemies.  Most mods are considerably cheaper.  Avoid paid mods that you cannot find positive reviews for or which look sketchy. 

Special note goes to the game's modular shipbuilding system.  If you grew up building Legos this will be the best part of Starfield for you.  When it starts to get old I recommend ship part and hab mods such as ASC Deimos, ASC Taiyo, Falkland, and Luxurious Ship Habs.  My God they're beautiful.

Bought the Digital Premium Edition and can't even play this POS without random crashes every 30-60 minutes. And when that's not happening, every other quicksave has a chance to crash the game too.

Who would've thunk that if you take a 15-year-old engine, slap a "2" on the end, and try to build a game on it, it would still run like garbage? Hell, even my 4,200-mod Skyrim build runs smoother than a clean install of this atrocity.

Someone hit me up when they fix this BS.

citations.review_text: Being a huge Bethesda fan, I really wanted to like this game. It has a lot of potential but really falls short of even being entertaining. It's worth stating that I have no problems running any other games in my library, but this one is incredibly buggy and the load times are absurd. The controls are difficult to remember and its easy to end up going through an endless string of menus just to find something, and even the menus take time to load. The missions can be kind of fun, but always feel short lived. Also, there is a weird bug that causes the dialog and video to be out of sync for the first thing an NPC says in a conversation. I asked for a return but they denied it as I played it for more than two hours, which is a little bit unfair because I spent half that time waiting for the thing to load.

The audio issues I've experienced in the short play time I have made this feel like a poorly dubbed movie, the frame rate issues on medium made the game unplayable. I would not recommed this game and it would take a Cyberpunk miracle to make me want to try it again.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that inventory management and menu navigation are clunky and confusing.

citations.review_text: Being a huge Bethesda fan, I really wanted to like this game. It has a lot of potential but really falls short of even being entertaining. It's worth stating that I have no problems running any other games in my library, but this one is incredibly buggy and the load times are absurd. The controls are difficult to remember and its easy to end up going through an endless string of menus just to find something, and even the menus take time to load. The missions can be kind of fun, but always feel short lived. Also, there is a weird bug that causes the dialog and video to be out of sync for the first thing an NPC says in a conversation. I asked for a return but they denied it as I played it for more than two hours, which is a little bit unfair because I spent half that time waiting for the thing to load.

Coming from someone with thousands of hours in Daggerfall, Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim I could not stomach playing for more than six hours before I got frustrated with the clunky inventory management, the crazy maze of menus they have you navigate to do simple things. 

Enemies and followers get stuck everywhere, or both simply stand still doing nothing during combat.
Ship to ship combat is tedious and not fun, which should be #1 priority in a space game.
No "real" space flight, everything is just loading screens


The straw that broke the camels back was the random ship encounter with spacers and a dead captain that attacks first, and defending yourself places a 15k+ bounty in UC space. Very fun to find out after fast traveling to the Lodge with an inventory full of loot.

Very slow story. I put about 5 hours and still struggled with finding a reason to care about the big starter event. The inventory UI is horrendous - it only allows you to view and sort one item attribute at a time. Want to compare item price, damage, and weight to decide what to sell? Well guess what. You need a mod for that. This game felt more like work than recreation. Waste of money. Not even worth it on sale.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe keybindings and control schemes as counterintuitive and awkward.

citations.review_text: It's just too messy to play. Tries to be simple yet it makes a lot of play just overly overloaded and stupid.

Not a terrible game. But since I lost interest after about 10 hours is is not worth the money. It's main problems are:
- Terrible controls: It's obviously a console game but most console games that are ported to PC do a way better job at adopting controls. (for example: I lost count of how ofter I accidently left the controls of the space ship and got out of my pilot chair because this is the same button as aiming at an enemy ship...for some reason someone thought that would be a good idea)
- Lack of motivation: While there is lots of stuff to do (exploration, ground combat, space combat, base building etc.) there is little reason to do any of it. The story and characters don't provide hooks and frankly I got bored after about 10 hours.
- The core gameplay elements are mediocre in quality. Ground combat (at normal difficulty, haven't tried others yet) is a bullet sponge shooting at bullet sponges, space combat suffers massively from poor controls and from the fast travel system. Base building is a grind with little revard that is locked behind perks that are locked behind other perks. Throughout that grind the player is mostly fighting the controls of the game or pressing the "always walk" button and mining minerals in between fast travelling.

Also the game design itself leans heavily into loading screen watching:
- fast travel to quest planet/station. (loading screen)
(-possibly a random encounter in space in which you are droped right on top of the enemies at the start rather than some distance away which would allow to use the elements in the game such as stealth, scanner, weapons with great range etc.)
- Land on planet (cutscene/loading screen)
- walk to quest marker and shoot bullet sponges. (fight against lack of QoL elements when it comes to inventory management)
- fast travel back to hand in quest (loading screen)
- fast travel to merchant A to sell stuff (2 loading screens, travelling + opening the door to the merchant)
- fast travel to merchan…

I don't recommend this game, quite frankly, right off the bat, the mouse sensitivity settings are not intuitive, somehow need more than one setting to actually make a difference, and unlike most games that have the X/Y attached to one slider, they force you to adjust ALL FOUR in addition to what should be the main slider.

The second major issue is that the keybinds are counterintuitive, some are forced to be bound together for no good reason, (See: flashlight and scanner. they have no business being together).
The menu navigation is also counterintuitive. The fact you can't use "ESC" to back out of ALL menus, is crazy. 

It's almost like Bethesda asked itself "How can I be different than other games, and really stand out?" "OH! I know, make the keybinds and menus hard to navigate and learn, then players will be forced to notice how different we are!"

Finally, setting up the buffs and debuffs supposedly didn't save, and I wouldn't have noticed if I hadn't been looking in to something else to notice it.  At which point... I was so frustrated by all the unnecessary ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, that I quit the game. 
I recognize I can change those settings at any time, but the fact I went through and already did it, only for it to not take, or somehow not save properly without some kind of OBVIOUS WARNING... again, it's because the menu navigation is counterintuitive for no reason.

And I really wanted to like this game. But, 2 hours in, I wasted so much of that time futzing around in the settings, and the countless misclicks or wasted time trying to find the right keybind.

And why drop me in to a planet, only to have me go back in the menu again and select the port? Why not drop me in, animate the move to the port, and let me dock? Why the extra steps?
Additionally, why drop me out on the far side of the planet, then have me manually move that planet in order to select the port I want. SO MANY EXTRA STEPS THAT WASTE TIME!

I am about to put the whole thing on easy mode just to make up…

I went into Starfield expecting a Bethesda game, and that is exactly what I got—for better and for worse.

At its best, I absolutely loved it. I played in 2026:

Pros: 
1) Dialogue is natural, so it feels more like you're speaking with people. But it's more The Office without Michael Scott or Dwight than discord mod.

2) Weapons and armor. Super fun to use, mix and match, and mod. The system combines the BEST parts of Fallout 4, the Outer Worlds, and add a research development/level system. So, you can't simply mod and improve everything if you haven't learned it and researched it.

3) The leveling system. Every level is 1 perk point. 84 skills with multiple tiers. In order to access the second and third tiers, you have to ACTUALLY do something (want to improve to Tier 2 Speech? Complete 3 successful conversation/persuasion events). I found this to be incredibly immersive since my ability to improve in something was DIRECTLY TIED to getting better at it. Also, with 84 skills, there is so much freedom to craft your player (this is called "role playing," and I find it particularly fun in a "role playing" game).

4) Ships. Flying. Modding. Living in them. Fighting with them. Docking and commandeering them. Super incredible and awesome systems that add to the normal "run, shoot, jump" combat and gameplay of many action RPGs. 

5) Exploration. Flying around. Driving the rover. Running around planets. Space is fun to scan and survey and explore, if you're into that. Want to produce your own materials? Go for it. I will say that these mechanics are not meant to be min/maxed, so just find spots and plop down because you will break it if you try to optimize it and it's not worth it. citations.review_text:
There are a few things Starfield does well. The ship-building system is genuinely fun, and designing, upgrading, and customizing ships was easily the highlight of my experience. If you enjoy tinkering with builds and creating your own spacecraft, there's a lot to like.

Unfortunately, that's where most of my praise ends.

The finished game feels nothing like what was marketed before release. The main quest is painfully boring—so much so that it almost feels intentional. I kept waiting for it to get interesting, but it never really did. The side quests aren't much better, with very few standing out as memorable.

Exploration is also a huge disappointment. The planets are mostly barren, and after a while you start seeing the same handful of points of interest repeated over and over. Instead of feeling like you're exploring a massive galaxy, it quickly becomes repetitive and lifeless.

For the price, I can't recommend it. If there were ever a AAA game that felt like the product of laziness and chasing profits over delivering a compelling experience, this would be near the top of the list.

My recommendation? Wait until it's heavily discounted. Maybe by 2036, if you can find it for around $3, it'll be worth checking out.

I really wanted a space Skyrim from Bethesda—spaceships instead of dragons, quests, a great story, and all the little details that make Bethesda games special.

I tried to play Starfield twice, but both times I ended up with the same result: it's just boring. When you see the same facility for the third time on the third planet, with the boss hiding in the exact same spot, you'll just uninstall it too.

The torpedos fired from the NPC with inflated stats stun the ship in 1 hit, effectively permanently disabling your ship with continued hits of these torpedos.

I will change my review if these issues are addressed in the future.

Pretty far into the main campaign and at most I find it to be just alright.  Now I haven't finished the main line yet so I could have a different opinion afterwards. So far each side story for the factions are engaging and different from one another and keeps everything interesting.

Exploration can be hit or miss.  Sometimes I feel like its a chore to run around a section of a planet just to discover something that is almost identical to others I've found.  However, there are some things that can be found and pull you back in.   Then I'll find myself spending hours running around a section just to identify everything.  Get the vehicle, which makes this process faster but sometimes I prefer running.  Controls of the vehicle can remind you of the Mako.

Speaking of the Mako, which I'm sure has been said before,  I feel Starfield is a mix of Fallout, No Man's Sky and Mass Effect.  Now I may be biased since the ME series is probably my favorite video game series and I'm also a massive Fallout fan with thousands of hours into both.  No Man's Sky I also enjoyed but put it down after maybe 50 or so hours and never returned, but plan to at some point.

Most of the time it is when I load the game and the title screen is playing.  Could be an issue with my system so who knows.  While in game, it has maybe happened 5 or 6 times which is pretty good for over 140 hours.
